niche-advanced__implement-strstr.title: Implement strStr()
niche-advanced__implement-strstr.pattern: KMP pattern matching with LPS (failure) array
niche-advanced__implement-strstr.statement: Return the index of the first occurrence of `needle` in `haystack`, or `-1` if it is not part of `haystack`.

examples.explanation: "sad" occurs at index 0 and 6; the first is 0.

constraints: haystack and needle consist of only lowercase English characters.

approaches.name: KMP (failure function)
approaches.idea: Build the longest-proper-prefix-that-is-also-suffix (LPS) array of `needle`, then scan `haystack` once. On a mismatch we fall back to `lps[j-1]` instead of re-scanning, so no character of the text is examined more than a constant number of times. This gives linear time regardless of how many partial matches occur.

niche-advanced__implement-strstr.insight: The LPS array lets you skip re-matching the prefix you already know matches, turning naive O(nm) into O(n+m).

niche-advanced__shortest-palindrome.title: Shortest Palindrome
niche-advanced__shortest-palindrome.pattern: KMP failure on s + '#' + reverse(s) to find longest palindromic prefix
niche-advanced__shortest-palindrome.statement: You are given a string `s`. You can convert `s` to a palindrome by adding characters in front of it. Return the shortest palindrome you can find by performing this transformation.
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters only.

approaches.name: KMP on s + '#' + reverse(s)
approaches.idea: The answer prepends the reverse of the non-palindromic suffix of `s`, so we need the longest prefix of `s` that is itself a palindrome. Concatenate `s + '#' + reverse(s)` and compute the LPS array; the final LPS value `k` is the length of the longest prefix of `s` equal to a suffix of `reverse(s)`, i.e. the longest palindromic prefix. The `#` separator prevents the match from overrunning `s`. Prepend `reverse(s.substring(k))`.

niche-advanced__shortest-palindrome.insight: Longest palindromic prefix = LPS of s + '#' + reverse(s); prepend the reverse of whatever is left over.

niche-advanced__repeated-substring-patte.title: Repeated Substring Pattern
niche-advanced__repeated-substring-patte.statement: Given a string `s`, check if it can be constructed by taking a substring of it and appending multiple copies of the substring together.
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters.

approaches.name: KMP failure length divisibility
approaches.idea: Let `k = lps[n-1]` be the longest proper prefix that is also a suffix. Then `n - k` is the length of the smallest repeating unit candidate. The string is a repetition iff `k > 0` and `n` is divisible by `n - k` — the period `n - k` tiles the whole string exactly.

niche-advanced__repeated-substring-patte.insight: The shortest period is n - lps[n-1]; the string repeats iff that period divides n.

niche-advanced__longest-happy-prefix.title: Longest Happy Prefix
niche-advanced__longest-happy-prefix.pattern: KMP LPS array; answer is the last LPS value
niche-advanced__longest-happy-prefix.statement: A string is called a happy prefix if it is a non-empty prefix which is also a suffix (excluding the string itself). Given a string `s`, return the longest happy prefix of `s`. Return an empty string if no such prefix exists.

examples.explanation: "l" is the longest prefix that is also a suffix.

constraints: s contains only lowercase English letters.

approaches.name: KMP failure function
approaches.idea: The longest happy prefix is exactly the definition of the last entry of the KMP LPS array: the longest proper prefix of `s` that is also a suffix. Build the LPS array in linear time and take the substring of that length.

niche-advanced__longest-happy-prefix.insight: This is literally the KMP failure value of the whole string: lps[n-1].

niche-advanced__find-all-anagrams.title: Find All Anagrams
niche-advanced__find-all-anagrams.pattern: Fixed-size sliding window with 26-letter frequency counts
niche-advanced__find-all-anagrams.statement: Given two strings `s` and `p`, return an array of all the start indices of `p`'s anagrams in `s`. You may return the answer in any order.
constraints: s and p consist of lowercase English letters.

approaches.name: Sliding window of frequency counts
approaches.idea: An anagram is a permutation, so any window of length `|p|` whose letter-frequency vector equals that of `p` is a match. Slide a window of fixed size `|p|` across `s`, adding the entering char and removing the exiting char in O(1), and compare the two 26-length count arrays at each valid position.

niche-advanced__find-all-anagrams.insight: Anagram search = fixed-width sliding window comparing 26-letter frequency vectors.

niche-advanced__distinct-echo-substrings.title: Distinct Echo Substrings
niche-advanced__distinct-echo-substrings.pattern: Double rolling hash (Rabin-Karp) over prefix hashes
niche-advanced__distinct-echo-substrings.statement: Return the number of distinct non-empty substrings of `text` that can be written as the concatenation of some string with itself (i.e. of the form `a + a`).
constraints: text has only lowercase English letters.

approaches.name: Prefix rolling hash + hash set
approaches.idea: A valid substring of half-length `len` starts at `i` iff the window `[i, i+len)` equals `[i+len, i+2len)`. Precompute polynomial prefix hashes so any substring hash is O(1). For every `len` and every start `i`, compare the two halves by hash; when equal, record the (double) hash of the half in a set so identical echo substrings are counted once. Two independent moduli make a false collision astronomically unlikely.

niche-advanced__distinct-echo-substrings.insight: Compare the two halves by O(1) prefix-hash lookups; dedupe echoes with a double-hash set.

niche-advanced__longest-duplicate-substr.title: Longest Duplicate Substring
niche-advanced__longest-duplicate-substr.pattern: Binary search on length + Rabin-Karp (double hashing)
niche-advanced__longest-duplicate-substr.statement: Given a string `s`, consider all duplicated substrings: (contiguous) substrings of `s` that occur 2 or more times. The occurrences may overlap. Return any duplicated substring that has the longest possible length. If `s` has no duplicated substring, return an empty string.
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters.

approaches.name: Binary search on length + rolling hash
approaches.idea: If a duplicate substring of length `L` exists, so does one of every smaller length, so the answer length is monotonic and can be binary-searched. For a candidate `L`, use Rabin-Karp: hash every length-`L` window (O(1) each via prefix hashes) and detect a repeated hash with a set. Double hashing makes collisions negligible, so a repeated key reliably signals a real duplicate. Track the start index of the found duplicate.

niche-advanced__longest-duplicate-substr.insight: Answer length is monotonic -> binary search it, testing each length with Rabin-Karp windows in a hash set.

niche-advanced__strings-differ-by-one-ch.title: Strings Differ by One Char
niche-advanced__strings-differ-by-one-ch.pattern: Positional polynomial hashing with masked-out column
niche-advanced__strings-differ-by-one-ch.statement: Given a list of strings `dict` where all the strings are of the same length, return `true` if there are two strings that differ by exactly one character in the same position, otherwise `false`.

examples.explanation: "abcd" and "aacd" differ only at index 1: 'b' vs 'a'.

constraints: dict[i] consists of only lowercase English letters.

approaches.name: Column-masked hashing with verification
approaches.idea: Two words differ at exactly one position `j` iff they are identical after deleting column `j`. Compute a polynomial hash of each word, then for each column `j` derive the masked hash by subtracting that column's contribution. Words sharing a masked hash at column `j` are identical except possibly at `j`; verify with a direct character diff (guards against hash collisions and against duplicate words, which differ by 0). Grouping per column keeps it linear in total characters.

niche-advanced__strings-differ-by-one-ch.insight: Mask out one column at a time via hash subtraction; equal masked hashes mean 'same except that column' -> verify one-char diff.

niche-advanced__fibonacci-at-large-n.title: Fibonacci at large n
niche-advanced__fibonacci-at-large-n.statement: Compute the `n`-th Fibonacci number modulo `10^9 + 7`, where `F(0) = 0`, `F(1) = 1`, and `F(k) = F(k-1) + F(k-2)`. `n` can be extremely large (up to 10^18), so a linear scan is too slow.

examples.explanation: Computed in O(log n) matrix multiplications.

approaches.name: Matrix fast exponentiation
approaches.idea: Since [[1,1],[1,0]]^n = [[F(n+1), F(n)], [F(n), F(n-1)]], raising the transformation matrix to the `n`-th power via binary exponentiation yields F(n) in the top-right cell. Squaring the matrix log(n) times reduces the recurrence from O(n) to O(log n), with all arithmetic done modulo 10^9 + 7.

niche-advanced__fibonacci-at-large-n.insight: Encode a linear recurrence as a matrix; matrix^n via binary exponentiation gives the n-th term in O(log n).

niche-advanced__count-paths-of-length-k-.title: Count paths of length k in a graph
niche-advanced__count-paths-of-length-k-.pattern: k-th power of the adjacency matrix
niche-advanced__count-paths-of-length-k-.statement: Given the adjacency matrix `adj` of a directed graph on `n` nodes (`adj[i][j] = 1` if there is an edge `i -> j`), a length `k`, and nodes `src` and `dst`, return the number of distinct walks of exactly `k` edges from `src` to `dst`, modulo `10^9 + 7`. Walks may repeat vertices and edges.

examples.explanation: The only length-3 walk 0->1->2->0 returns to 0.

constraints: adj[i][j] is 0 or 1; answer returned modulo 10^9 + 7.

approaches.name: Adjacency matrix power
approaches.idea: The number of walks of length exactly `k` from `i` to `j` equals `(A^k)[i][j]`, where `A` is the adjacency matrix — this follows by induction, since one matrix multiply extends every walk by one edge. Compute `A^k` by binary exponentiation of the matrix, giving O(n^3 log k) instead of enumerating exponentially many walks.

niche-advanced__count-paths-of-length-k-.insight: Walks of length k between nodes = entries of A^k; exponentiate the adjacency matrix in O(log k).

niche-advanced__knight-dialer.title: Knight Dialer
niche-advanced__knight-dialer.pattern: Linear DP over digit transitions; matrix power for huge n
niche-advanced__knight-dialer.statement: A chess knight sits on a phone dialpad (digits 0-9 in the usual layout, with `*` and `#` unusable). Starting on any numeric cell, the knight makes `n - 1` valid knight moves to dial a number of length `n`. Return how many distinct phone numbers of length `n` can be dialed, modulo `10^9 + 7`.

examples.explanation: Each of the 10 digits is a valid length-1 number.

approaches.name: Linear DP over knight transitions
approaches.idea: Let `dp[d]` be the count of length-`L` numbers ending on digit `d`. Each digit reaches a fixed small set of digits by a knight move, so `next[nb] += dp[d]` for every neighbor `nb`. Starting from `dp[d] = 1` (length 1), iterate `n - 1` times and sum. Linear in `n` with only 10 states.

approaches.name: Matrix exponentiation (for astronomically large n)
approaches.idea: The transition is linear, so build a 10x10 matrix `T` with `T[nb][d] = 1` when digit `d` can move to `nb`. Then the vector of counts after `n - 1` steps is `T^(n-1)` applied to the all-ones vector; summing its entries gives the answer. Raising `T` to a power via binary exponentiation makes this O(10^3 log n), which matters if `n` were up to 10^18 rather than 5000.

niche-advanced__knight-dialer.insight: Knight moves form a fixed linear transition on 10 digits: O(n) DP, or matrix^(n-1) when n is enormous.

niche-advanced__student-attendance-recor.title: Student Attendance Record II
niche-advanced__student-attendance-recor.pattern: DP over (absences, trailing lates) states; matrix power variant
niche-advanced__student-attendance-recor.statement: An attendance record of length `n` is a string of `'A'` (absent), `'L'` (late), `'P'` (present). A record is rewardable if it contains fewer than 2 `'A'` total and never has 3 or more consecutive `'L'`. Return the number of rewardable records of length `n`, modulo `10^9 + 7`.

examples.explanation: All length-2 strings except "AA" are rewardable.

approaches.name: DP over 6 states (absences x trailing lates)
approaches.idea: State = (number of `A` so far in {0,1}, number of trailing `L` in {0,1,2}), 6 states total. From each state: appending `P` resets lates to 0; appending `A` is allowed only if no `A` yet and resets lates to 0; appending `L` is allowed only if fewer than 2 trailing lates and increments them. Iterate `n` times and sum all states.

approaches.name: Matrix exponentiation over the 6 states
approaches.idea: Because the state transition is fixed and linear, flatten the 6 states into a vector and encode the P/A/L transitions in a 6x6 matrix `T`. The answer is the sum of entries of `T^n` applied to the initial state, computable in O(6^3 log n) — the standard speedup when `n` is far larger than 10^5.

niche-advanced__student-attendance-recor.insight: Track (total A, trailing L) as 6 states: O(n) DP, and the same transition as a 6x6 matrix^n for huge n.

niche-advanced__number-of-ways-to-stay-i.title: Number of Ways to Stay in the Same Place After Some Steps
niche-advanced__number-of-ways-to-stay-i.pattern: Bounded DP over reachable positions (capped at steps/2)
niche-advanced__number-of-ways-to-stay-i.statement: You have a pointer at index 0 in an array of size `arrLen`. At each step you may move the pointer 1 position left, 1 position right, or stay, without ever leaving the array bounds. Given `steps` and `arrLen`, return the number of ways to move the pointer so that after exactly `steps` steps it is back at index 0, modulo `10^9 + 7`.

examples.explanation: Right/Left/Stay combinations: RLS, RSL, SRL, SSS.

approaches.name: DP over reachable positions
approaches.idea: To return to index 0 within the remaining steps, the pointer can never go farther right than `steps/2`, so cap positions at `maxPos = min(steps/2, arrLen-1)` even when the array is huge. Let `dp[p]` be the number of ways to be at position `p`; each step spreads a position's count to itself, left, and right (respecting bounds). After `steps` iterations, `dp[0]` is the answer.

niche-advanced__number-of-ways-to-stay-i.insight: Cap reachable index at steps/2 (not arrLen) so the DP is O(steps^2) even for a million-length array.
